analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon emissions and returns the money through household rebates and infrastructure spending.
analysis.headline: The carbon-tax-and-rebate bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a $49-per-ton tax on the carbon dioxide content of coal, oil, and natural gas, rising each year with inflation plus two points. The money would flow into a dedicated fund: large annual amounts for highways, transit, rail, aviation, harbors, flood control, clean water, and broadband; $5 billion a year for coal-country workers and communities; monthly cash refunds for low-income households; and a refundable tax credit for working families up to 350% of the poverty line. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower-income households (those under 150% of poverty, such as SNAP and SSI recipients) would get monthly energy refunds sized to cover the higher energy costs the tax causes. Working families up to 350% of the poverty line would get a refundable tax credit. Coal miners and community residents would get $5 billion a year for retraining, pensions, health benefits, and mine cleanup. Drivers, transit riders, and communities would get new infrastructure spending, funded by the tax rather than by borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households, coal communities, and infrastructure users

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $49 tax per metric ton of carbon dioxide content on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas starting in 2019, rising annually with inflation plus two percentage points, with the revenue dedicated to a Build America Trust Fund.

Creates an Energy Refund Program paying monthly cash refunds to households at or below 150% of the poverty line, including SNAP, SSI, and low-income Medicare beneficiaries, sized to cover their estimated loss in purchasing power from the tax.
Creates a refundable 'working families relief' tax credit for households up to 350% of the poverty line, funded out of the carbon tax revenue, with larger credits for larger families.

Directs roughly $50 billion a year plus any highway shortfall to highways and transit, $3 billion to aviation, $5 billion to passenger rail, $6 billion to harbors, waterways, flood protection and dams, $4.4 billion to clean water and drinking water funds, about $1 billion to USDA rural water programs, and $3 billion a year to broadband deployment, for fiscal years 2019 through 2028.

Sets aside $5 billion a year for workers and communities reliant on coal and other carbon-intensive industries, including worker retraining, pension and health benefits, abandoned mine reclamation, and carbon capture technology development.
Includes border adjustment fees on carbon-intensive imports and rebates for exports, so domestic manufacturers are not undercut by foreign producers that face no carbon tax.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers pay the tax directly and would pass much of it through to consumers in higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Middle- and upper-income households get no rebate and would bear those higher costs net. Energy-intensive manufacturers pay more for fuel, offset only if the border adjustment is implemented well.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and middle-income energy consumers

drawbacks.text: A carbon tax raises prices on gasoline, heating oil, and electricity for every household; the bill fully offsets only low-income households and those under 350% of the poverty line, so middle-income families would pay more on net.

The border adjustment on imports relies on the Treasury Secretary to identify carbon-intensive goods and calculate equivalent fees, a mechanism that could be administered loosely or challenged by trading partners.

The energy refund and consumer rebate depend on annual estimates of households' purchasing-power loss and on available trust fund money; if the fund falls short, the bill directs pro-rata cuts to the monthly refunds.

The bill had no Republican cosponsors, so its sponsors' preferred design — tax collected at the top of the supply chain and rebated to households — never faced the committee scrutiny and negotiation that a law would have required.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households below 350% of the poverty line the design is deliberately protective: the tax's costs to them are refunded in cash. The people left bearing the cost are middle- and upper-income households and fossil fuel producers, which is the point of the tax. The infrastructure and coal-community spending are real and funded, not borrowed. The main honest objections are the middle-class net cost, the reliance on administrative estimates for the refunds, and the fact that the border adjustment's effectiveness depends entirely on how Treasury writes the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to seven House committees and a handful of subcommittees, but none ever held a markup or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on November 1, 2017, with 16 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and six other committees, and then to subcommittees on aviation, highways and transit, railroads, water resources, environment, and energy.
Over the remaining fourteen months of the 115th Congress, no committee reported the bill, no markup was held, and no vote was ever scheduled in the House.
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, and no Republican support.
The bill died on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended without any action on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users were better off because the bill died: no carbon tax was ever imposed on coal, oil, and natural gas, and no funding mechanism for the rebates and infrastructure ever took effect. Households that would have received the energy refunds and tax credits got nothing, and the higher-energy costs were never offset either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, because no tax was imposed

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, pairing a carbon tax with household refunds, coal-community aid, and infrastructure spending.

for.name: 21 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, the committee with primary jurisdiction over its tax provisions.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.role: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
against.what_they_did: Opposed carbon-tax legislation as a class during this period; no producer or trade group supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the House never took the bill up.

industries.note: The tax is levied directly on coal's carbon content, and $5 billion a year of the revenue goes to coal workers and communities for retraining, pensions, and mine cleanup. Coal producers would bear the largest direct burden of any industry, and the bill's failure left coal regions without that transition assistance.

Petroleum products and natural gas are taxed on their carbon dioxide content at the manufacturer, producer, or importer level, raising the cost of their products. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the rebates and infrastructure spending it would have funded.

More than $70 billion a year would flow to highways, transit, rail, aviation, harbors, water projects, and clean water for a decade, creating contracts and construction work. Communities would get the roads, rails, and water systems themselves.
$3 billion a year is set aside for broadband deployment with an emphasis on unserved communities, expanding the customer base and construction work for network builders.

industries.industry: Public transit and passenger rail operators
industries.note: The bill funds transit accounts, the Northeast Corridor, and rail state-of-good-repair grants that transit agencies and Amtrak have historically struggled to obtain.

They would pay more for fuel, but the bill imposes carbon-equivalency fees on comparable imports and refunds the tax on exports specifically to keep them competitive, and the infrastructure spending benefits their shipping and supply chains.
